paras.en: Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s You Can See Everything is a strong draw for younger audiences, with the turnout showing 75 percent of ticket buyers in New York and Los Angeles as under age 35. Critics and general attendees alike have marveled at You Can See Everything, and it boasts a 99 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes from both reviewers and audiences. It stands as the highest-rated Letterboxd title ever with a 4.8 score.

Universal Pictures’ Other Mommy could be heading for third place with around $7.8 million, marking a sharp decline of about 72 percent after earning a D+ CinemaScore in last weekend’s debut. Jessica Chastain stars as a sinister spirit appearing in a girl’s closet in Rob Savage’s horror offering that heads to an estimated domestic sum of $43.3 million after opening at No. 1 a week ago.

Getting a quiet start is 20th Century Studios’ Whalefall, which is expected to reel in around $7 million from 3,065 North American theaters. This is below the $11 million that the studio was projecting for director Brian Duffield’s survival thriller starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale. Earning a B CinemaScore from audiences, Whalefall carries a $60 million budget for the feature adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel.

Whalefall holds a 71 percent critics approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with an 82 score from audiences. THR chief film critic David Rooney wrote in his review that the movie is “just not batshit crazy enough to be much fun.”

Coming in just below that on the chart is Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibility, which took in $3.2 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, for an estimated opening of $6.7 million from 2,545 North American theaters. Earning an A- CinemaScore, director Georgia Oakley’s adaptation of Jane Austen‘s esteemed novel stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in the story of the Dashwood sisters navigating life after their father’s death.

Carrying a budget in the mid-$20 millions, Sense and Sensibility holds a 75 percent approval from Rotten Tomatoes critics and an 89 score from audiences. Rooney noted that the film “seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling.”
Additionally, Netflix releases buzzy Oscar contender La Bola Negra in four theaters, with this title marking the first time ever that the streamer will publicly release box office returns.
The options heading to theaters next weekend include Clayface, Wildwood, Klara and the Sun, Ali G: Who Iz I? and Wicker.

articles.title: Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets

paras.en: When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber.
The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage.

Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term.

"Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy.
"Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said.

Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially.
Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor.

Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said.

For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial, has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers, providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting.

The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation.
Timberland managers dominate acquisitions
Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue.

According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently.

Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said.

According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall.

South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%. Pine sawtimber prices fell about 6% over the same period, from $22.78 to $21.47 a ton, while hardwood sawtimber prices rose about 40%, from $16.04 to $22.52.

Historically, pulpwood has been as high as $12 to $18 a ton, according to Dorn, and twenty years ago, soft timber was in the $35-$40 range. He said those prices could make a comeback if the housing market ever recovers, because pine sawtimber is cut into lumber for new homes, so its price tends to follow home building.

Strategically placed, timber may not be a bad investment, according to Dorn, though that would be because of the land itself more than the timber. "The return is in the land, not the timber," Dorn said.

He advises anyone thinking of investing in timberland to scout for prime parcels of land located outside growing metro areas that may be poised to pop as the local population keeps spreading. "If one hopes to buy land near growing metro areas and holds on to it, timber is a reasonable way to keep it earning something — a very low return — while you hold that land," he said.

Michael Martin, a timber owner in western New York and vice president of market strategy at brokerage firm TradingBlock, says timberland can be a good long-term investment but the reality of being an owner belies the romantic image of acres of untouched timberland. It is not as passive an investment class as it may seem to be.

Direct ownership is highly illiquid and comes with management costs, property taxes, harvesting expenses, exposure to local timber markets, and risks including wildfire, pests, disease and trespassers hunting or cutting trees.

And when it is time to harvest timber, you need to make sure you are getting the best deal. "If you simply go with a small local outfit without getting competing bids, you don't always know if you're getting the best price," Martin said.
He also said timber prices are very local and can impact whether it's a solid investment.
"I am constantly checking stumpage reports because timber prices are extremely local. An oak tree in western New York may have a completely different value from one in the Adirondacks," Martin said.
In addition, partial timbering every ten years or so has barely covered the property taxes. "At the end of the day, I barely break even," he added.
Some in local real estate and investing markets say younger buyers are curious, though firsthand evidence is hard to find.

"As a millennial and a realtor, I understand the appeal. I've thought about buying timberland myself," said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based realtor, noting that his generation has lived through the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, a pandemic, huge swings in housing and now inflation. "One lesson from all of that we have learned is that scarcity matters when it comes to places to park your money," Kennedy said, adding as examples that more IPOs can be announced or new crypto created.

"But you can't manufacture another 500 acres of land," Kennedy said. "Timber itself is a resource that takes decades to grow. And there is something reassuring about owning an asset that is tangible," he added. But he also cautioned that timber's durability doesn't mean profitability. Trees can be temperamental and subject to many variables.

The people Kennedy has spoken with see timberland as a relatively safe place to park money, he said, because demand for timber products isn't going away. "In the meantime, yes, hunting is a common activity while owners are waiting for the investment to grow and mature, literally," he said.

"I don't think my generation is suddenly giving up on houses and becoming timber barons. However, I do think we are a lot more interested in alternative places to store wealth than previous generations might have been," he added.
Timber ETFs offer access to the asset class

For many millennials, homeownership has become increasingly difficult due to elevated home prices, higher mortgage rates, and limited inventory in many markets. "As a result, some investors are looking for alternative ways to participate in real assets and potentially build equity without purchasing a home directly," said Nadeem Kassam, chief investment strategist at Marnoa Private Wealth Counsel.

Outside direct or institutional fund ownership, there are timber ETFs and timber-focused funds that provide exposure to a theme that is closely tied to long-term housing demand and construction activity, though they remain highly niche investments in an ETF market now valued in the trillions of dollars.
Kassam pointed to the iShares Global Timber & Forestry ETF (WOOD), with roughly $260 million in assets, and the Invesco MSCI Global Timber ETF (CUT), which has roughly $30 million in assets.

"The investment case is supported by persistent housing shortages across many parts of the U.S. and growing bipartisan support for policies aimed at increasing housing supply and improving affordability. If these efforts lead to increased homebuilding over time, demand for lumber and wood products could benefit," Kassam said.
But he noted that investors should understand that timber ETFs are not a direct investment in timberland. Neither ETF owns trees.

"Most own publicly traded companies involved in timber, forest products, wood manufacturing, and other parts of the housing value chain," Kassam said, explaining the advantage is liquidity and accessibility, but returns will be driven by more than just timber prices.

WOOD's largest holdings include Weyerhaeuser, a major timberland owner, alongside Brazilian pulp maker Suzano, Nine Dragons Paper and West Fraser Timber. CUT is weighted toward paper, packaging and materials makers such as Svenska Cellulosa, UPM, Stora Enso and Avery Dennison. WOOD has drawn about $73 million in net inflows over the past year, according to ETF Database.

"For investors who are priced out of the housing market, timber ETFs may offer a way to participate in the long-term housing and construction story through a diversified, liquid investment vehicle. The key is recognizing that you're buying exposure to businesses that benefit from housing-related demand, not a direct ownership stake in land or residential real estate," Kassam said.

Junyi Liu, professor of economics at Soka University of America, who studies international and development economics, said he is not seeing evidence of a boom, but that timberland does have some unusual characteristics as an alternative asset.

"Returns can come from biological growth, timber prices, and land appreciation, and owners sometimes have the option to delay harvesting when timber prices are unfavorable," Liu said. But for retail investors, Liu added, it is quite different from "the simple 'trees grow while you wait' investment story."

articles.title: 'Dead money’ for a decade: Why this hedge fund approach may deliver an advantage over bonds

paras.en: Investors may want to rethink their bond allocation and opt for managed futures exposure.
DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios.

"[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't."

Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility, which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade.
His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events.

"You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that."

He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF). The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website.

"There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio."
As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data.
However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds.
According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio.

"I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation."
Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio.
These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance.
"You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."

articles.title: Software’s new consolidator gets big vote of confidence from Berkshire

paras.en: At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.

Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway.

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."

Shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."

Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus.
Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo, AOL and Eventbrite in 2025.
The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.

Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.
Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."
"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.
Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."
As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.
"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."
Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.

"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."
For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.

In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.
"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.
"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."
Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.
"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.
For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.

The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.

That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.
On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.

Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.
"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

articles.title: Can AI break encryption? OpenAI’s new math has cryptographers divided

paras.en: Last week OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, dropped 722 mathematical manuscripts online in one go, every one of them penned by an artificial intelligence model unavailable to the public. The output was far from perfect: OpenAI withdrew three of the papers within a day, and mathematicians are still poring over the rest. But the scale of the research, and the incisiveness of its insights, has some worried.

Math powers cryptography. Every text you send and every bank log-in you submit is protected by a math problem that’s supposedly impossible to crack. The system rests on the assumption that no one will figure out how. And AI just showed it’s pretty good at math.

That worries Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University. In a social media post a few days after OpenAI’s massive math release, he suggested there was a 15 percent chance that we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms—which allow computers to establish secure connections and verify digital identities without first exchanging a shared secret key.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

That confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to break those algorithms. Take elliptic curve cryptography, used across the Internet and by cryptocurrencies. Its security relies on the belief that there’s no efficient algorithm capable of reversing the mathematical operations at its core. But if AI can spot shortcuts that humans have missed, that belief could be proven wrong.

Humans have found such shortcuts before, Green says. An algorithm called the number field sieve made it far easier to crack RSA, another widely used public-key system, when it relied on 512-bit keys. Cryptographers responded by lengthening the keys, and 2,048 bits is now considered the minimum. Another advance on that scale “could potentially seriously reduce the security level of the schemes that we standardize,” he says.

Govind Pimpale, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, thinks AI could make the next one more likely. Public-key cryptography depends on relatively few mathematical problems, he says, each studied by a comparatively small community. Machines could throw vastly more effort at them and find flaws or faster algorithms that would let attackers work out secret keys from public ones. “Public-key cryptography is necessary for essentially all online commerce and secure messaging, so its loss would have dire consequences,” he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Plenty of others disagree that AI will break modern encryption. Yehuda Lindell, a professor at Bar-Ilan University in Israel and head of cryptography at Coinbase, wrote on X that there is “no evidence whatsoever” of a breakthrough against the mathematical problems underlying those systems. Nor does a single one of OpenAI’s 722 papers deal with cryptography, which Dan Boneh, a professor of computer science at Stanford University, calls “a little striking.”

Still, Green’s worry is not entirely hypothetical. In a recent preprint, Florian Tramèr, a computer scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich, and his colleagues—three of them at the AI company Anthropic—pitted leading AI models against 191 code-breaking challenges. “It’s pretty clear that models’ ability in cryptanalysis is growing extremely rapidly,” Tramèr says. In summer 2025 the researchers weren’t even sure AI could reproduce relatively simple attacks. Months later, the models were turning up weaknesses no one had spotted before. Anthropic has also reported that its Claude model found a substantially improved attack on HAWK, a proposed digital signature scheme designed to withstand quantum computers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But there’s a huge gulf between finding weaknesses in experimental cryptography and breaking the systems that secure large parts of our digital lives. “Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes. The bigger concern is a shortcut that cracks an entire family of mathematical problems at once, and with it every system built on them.

Public-key cryptography secures the connection between your browser and the sites you visit, and it produces the digital signatures that certify a software update or a cryptocurrency transaction. Crack it, and attackers could pose as your bank or listen in on your messages. Anyone who has stockpiled encrypted traffic could go back and read it years after the senders assumed it was safe.

Even then, it wouldn’t necessarily signal disaster. Bart Preneel, a cryptography professor at the Catholic University of Leuven (KU Leuven) in Belgium, says the consequences would depend on the scale of any breakthrough. A modest mathematical advance might dent the protection offered by existing systems but not break it. Even making an attack a billion times faster might still leave it requiring more computing power than anyone could realistically muster, AI or no AI. “I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Even a modest advance would necessitate a defense upgrade, and Green thinks that that could do damage of its own. “The upgrade process itself is going to be a bit of a catastrophe,” he says. “We screw up the upgrade, and we end up with something insecure accidentally.”

Eyal Ronen, a researcher at Tel Aviv University, who co-authored the cryptanalysis study, is, like Preneel, cautious. AI is already very good at finding software vulnerabilities, he says, which presents a much more immediate threat than the hypothetical disappearance of encryption. And any hacker is more likely to take the easier route, such as hacking someone’s computer to steal their encryption keys, than to try breaking the mathematics protecting them.

Efforts to prepare for quantum computers, another potential threat, are already forcing governments and companies to rethink their encryption. Boneh says those efforts could help if AI discovers something unexpected, although the two threats aren’t identical. HAWK, after all, was built for the quantum era, yet AI found a way to weaken it.

For now, Boneh wants something relatively straightforward from AI companies: greater transparency about what their models have tried and how often they’ve succeeded. Green agrees. “We’re getting no signal whatsoever,” he says. If the labs have pointed their models at the mathematical problems underpinning cryptography, saying so would help reassure the people responsible for securing the Internet. “Please tell us what you have discovered when you tried some cryptography questions,” Boneh says. Until someone does, nobody can say whether AI has exposed something fundamental about the mathematics we rely on—or whether it’s simply getting better at solving problems that were always solvable.

articles.title: Scientists discover an ancient shipwreck dating to when the Great Pyramid was built

paras.en: They don’t make ’em like they used to. A shipwreck believed to date to the early Bronze Age has been discovered at the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea, where it has remained sitting, complete with intact cargo.
The small boat was first found in 2024 by scientists at Türkiye’s Akdeniz University. A blip on their sonar screen led them to the remains, which were surrounded by three stone anchors.

While old shipwrecks in the area aren’t uncommon, most have dated to roughly 2,000 to 1,500 years ago, during the Roman or Byzantine eras. This ship, however, is far older, likely dating to the early Bronze Age, when the Hattian civilization was beginning to form. The scientists believe the remains are between 4,700 and 4,400 years old. That would make this the oldest shipwreck ever found, surpassing the previous contender by centuries.

Inside the ship, the archaeologists found around 18 remarkably intact, flat-bottomed containers called amphorae, which were commonly used to store and transport liquids such as olive oil and wine at the time. Some of the containers were marked with finely etched symbols, although what they mean is not yet clear.

The unfortunate crew of the doomed vessel were likely sailing to the west when disaster struck, the researchers wrote in a study about the wreck that was published earlier this year. The area where it was found has strong currents that can be treacherous when combined with wind, they noted.

Türkiye’s culture minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy posted a video of the underwater site on social media on Wednesday. In the post, Ersoy said the shipwreck sheds light “on the deep-rooted history of maritime trade along the Anatolian coasts.”
“We continue to illuminate Anatolia’s maritime history with new discoveries, preserving our underwater cultural heritage to pass it on to future generations,” he said.

articles.title: Plants move to get away from their decaying brethren

paras.en: Plants seem stationary: they don’t skip, fly or walk around. But that doesn’t mean they don’t move. The organisms bend their roots and shoots in response to stimuli such as water, light, salt and gravity. These responsive movements, called tropisms, are crucial for plants’ survival.
Now researchers have discovered a new way plants move, which they call “saprotropism”: the bending of roots to avoid dead or rotting plant tissue. The results were published in Science.

The discovery began with a failed experiment and an unexpected observation. Yuzhou Zhang, a biologist at Northwest A&F University in China, was studying how plants move in response to gravity in a laboratory in Austria when one of his agar plates became contaminated with airborne microbes. Just before he threw it away, he noticed something striking: almost every single one of the plants’ roots in the plate was bent away from the spoilage. The consistency “immediately made me wonder whether this was more than a random response,” Zhang says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

His team decided to investigate further. The researchers grew the common research plant Arabidopsis thaliana in containers, some of which were dotted with patches of rotting apple. The plants that encountered “decay zones” bent their roots to avoid the bad apple, whereas the ones in containers lacking decay grew straight through. Repeating the experiment with other plants, including tomatoes and wheat, yielded similar results—but an encounter with putrefying animal tissues had no effect. Zhang and his colleagues theorize that this reaction might help plants avoid pathogens, similar to the way unpleasant smells help animals steer clear of rotten food.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Saprotropism seems to operate differently than most other plant tropisms. “It does not follow the classical mechanism,” Zhang says. For example, gravitropism, or movement in response to gravity, and phototropism—in response to light—occur when plants redistribute the hormone auxin in their stems or roots, causing them to change their growth direction.

In contrast, saprotropism relies on a hormone called abscisic acid (ABA). When the plant roots encounter an area acidified by decaying plant matter—a chemical gradient distinct from that of animal matter—ABA builds up on the side facing the rot, encouraging growth in the other direction.

The work’s scope is impressive, says Chris Wolverton, a plant biologist at Ohio Wesleyan University, who was not involved in the study. He adds, however, that “there’s still a lot of open space in the signaling mechanism for more detail to get fleshed out.” At what point, for instance, does decaying plant tissue break down enough to become nutritious compost?
Zhang’s team hopes to fill those gaps in future studies. Ultimately the research could help illuminate how plants sense and interact with the world around them.

articles.title: Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.

I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.

Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.

In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.

Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.

The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.

But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.

Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”

On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?

Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.

“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”

Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.
The Deep End podcast explores what makes your voice yours

What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.

By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.

From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.

A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”

Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.

Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.

After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”
Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.

Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”

Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.
Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”

Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”
But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.

The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.
“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”
Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them into

words. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.

Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.

But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.
For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.

“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”

Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”

Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.

The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neurosurgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.

Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Paradromics’ priority is to test whether the implant is safe. If so, scientists can turn to the goal of restoring speech in real time. “The moment that you’re thinking the words, you don’t have to wait for the sentence to complete,” says Willsey, who, like Brandman, is a site investigator for the Paradromics clinical trial. “You can let the words kind of flow out as they would in a normal conversation.”

Scientists also want to decode more than words. Qualities of voice, such as pitch, are important for marking questions, says Vikash Gilja, a Paradromics neuroscientist. Speakers can also alter or pace their conversation to show sarcasm or concern. These sounds are all made by moving muscles, Gilja says, and can therefore be decoded from the brain.

“Our near-term goal right now is just to restore speech,” says Paradromics neurosurgeon Stephen Ryu. “But eventually, we’re hoping that we can actually restore someone’s ability to be fully involved in a conversation, to basically decode things like their timing, their emotions, their personality.”
Other researchers are trying to incorporate the gestures that many of us use to communicate.

“Some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up,” says bioengineer Samantha Brosler of the University of California, San Fransico. Gestures can also change the meaning of words; a “maybe” with a head nod is close to a yes, for instance. “I think of gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech,” Brosler says.

In a new study, Brosler and colleagues enabled two people with paralysis who had lost their speaking ability to instead use their brain signals to control both the words and gestures of digital avatars. The advance, reported in September in Nature Neuroscience, adds to the repertoire of signals that could be decoded and turned into action.

And as all this is happening, scientists are creating smaller, more stable types of electrodes to embed in the brain; more powerful computational algorithms to handle larger amounts of data; and better models of how those signals relate to sounds, words and gestures, Gilja says. “We can see all the pieces coming together.”

There are many reasons to be optimistic about the future, says Brandman, who is an investigator for the clinical trial led by Paradromics. “I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation,” he says. “‘Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate.’”

That conversation is tantalizing. But there are no guarantees that these systems will work as hoped, or that they will be widely available. Such implants would probably come with hefty price tags, invasive brain surgeries and perhaps more demand than the few capable clinicians and technologists could meet.

And there are underlying questions about the brain itself. One concern is that changes to the brain over time might render neural signals unreliable, especially as diseases progress. If that happens, a person’s interface might produce a scrambled message — or be left without enough neural data to decode.
“These are real challenges, and the field is working on them,” Stavisky says. “But they’re not solved yet.”

Despite these hurdles, the push for voice-restoring technology can’t come soon enough for people who have lost theirs. In September, researchers reported that the woman with the Paradromics implant had a message for them. “OK,” she used her brain-computer interface to tell researchers. “I have a lot to say.” With her system, she was able to call her grandchildren on the telephone.

And Harrell is now living a life that looks very different from the one he might have imagined six years ago. Although his disease keeps him close to home, he can now share his thoughts with the world — and his family — instead of locking them away inside.

“The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress, the ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear,” Harrell says. “These are the things that life is all about, and when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now.”
But he too has a vision, a day when these devices are commonplace, “when I am one of many, instead of being one of one.”
For more about the human voice and to hear from Casey Harrell himself, listen to The Deep End podcast Season Two, called Talk to Me. It’s free wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title: A telling hole in a Neandertal bone hints at a bitter end
articles.author: Freda Kreier

paras.en: A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.

The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.

These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.

Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.

During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.

At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.
The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.

Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.

The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.
The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.

The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.

“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

articles.title: Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient
articles.author: Aimee Cunningham

paras.en: Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.

The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.

Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.

“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”
Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.

With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”

When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.

In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.

Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.

Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.

There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290 mcg for those breastfeeding. The amount of the nutrient that iodized salt contains can vary, but will be listed on the container’s label. Based on a 2023 federal report on food iodine content, one teaspoon of salt has around 300 mcg of added iodine. (The American Heart Association recommends a limit of 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day; one teaspoon of salt has 2,400 mg of sodium.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The American Thyroid Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that pregnant and breastfeeding people, as well as those planning to become pregnant, take a daily supplement with 150 micrograms of iodine. Sufficient iodine is especially important in the first trimester of pregnancy, when a developing embryo relies solely on the mother’s supply.

When choosing table salt, “look for salt that’s iodized,” Pearce says. For people on a low-salt diet, it’s better to cut out packaged and prepared foods, Serrano-Gonzalez says. “We do want to have moderation with salt intake, but we need a little bit” of iodized salt, she says.

People have largely forgotten why it’s important to choose iodized salt, Pearce says. It’s not a decision that many people have to make globally: One hundred and twenty-six countries mandate salt iodization, while only 21 have voluntary polices.

An observational study of an iodine crisis in Ethiopia indicates the catastrophic consequences of losing the nutrient. The country adopted a salt iodization policy in the 1990s, and by 1995, 80 percent of households reported using iodized salt. But the country’s stock came from Eritrea, and in 1998, a conflict between the two countries closed the border and interrupted the supply of iodized salt. By 2005, the Ethiopian population was severely iodine deficient, with up to 40 percent of school-aged children and 36 percent of women of reproductive age developing goiters. Ethiopia’s government was able to reinstate mandatory salt iodization in 2012, and household coverage climbed to 85 percent by 2015.

paras.en: But the severe iodine disruption during the war had a devastating effect on the children born and raised in that period. In rural areas, which had very low soil iodine levels, mortality among children in the first two years of life reached 25 to 30 percent, compared with 10 percent in other areas, researchers reported in Nature Food in September. The children from rural areas who reached secondary school scored lower on national exams. The study team took other effects of the conflict into account, to focus on the impact of the iodine nutrition emergency.
