articles.title: Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss

paras.en: Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
The United Nations Secretary-General appealed on Friday for governments, businesses and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations and all life on Earth.
Guterres was speaking in Yerevan, Armenia, ahead of the opening of the COP17 UN biodiversity conference next week.
“The food we eat, the water we drink, the very air we breathe – all are the gifts of biodiversity,” he told the Leaders’ Summit. “Yet every day, humankind saws another branch off the tree of life.”

The UN chief said factors such as climate disruption, overgrazing and excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides “are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos”.
As a result, more than a million species face the risk of extinction, “edging us ever closer towards an uninhabitable world,” he warned, adding that “it doesn’t have to be this way”.
Mr. Guterres said the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed four years ago, had inspired action worldwide.

Nearly 90 per cent of parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than half have developed national road maps. Since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.

However, “progress is uneven, and far too slow”, he said. Even if countries fulfil their current commitments, only 26 per cent of terrestrial ecosystems and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030 – “well short” of the Framework’s goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by that date.

He also highlighted “major gaps” in national targets linked to economic systems, including commitments to reduce incentives that harm nature. Finance, technical capacity, cooperation and data collection remain inadequate, he said, noting that biodiversity financing is less than half of the $200 billion agreed under the Framework.

He stressed that biodiversity cannot be treated separately from conflict, food insecurity, disease threats or climate change. “Addressing any of these crises requires addressing them all,” he said. “And there is no time to waste.”
The Secretary-General first called for government leadership, urging countries to meet the “30 by 30” target and “shift from policies that destroy nature, to practices that sustain it”.
Priorities include zero-waste and circular economies, sustainable farming, regenerative agriculture, stronger monitoring and transparency and firmer enforcement of existing laws.
He welcomed the Yerevan Declaration and its commitment to integrate biodiversity into government policies, budgets and regulations.

His second appeal focused on finance as “the stark truth is, we are spending money on the wrong things”. He noted that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, $30 is spent on activities that damage it.
“In 2023, $7.3 trillion flowed into nature-negative industries,” he said, including polluting heavy industry, destructive agribusiness and fossil fuels.
“I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”

The Secretary-General said that meeting global biodiversity, climate and land-restoration goals would require annual investment in nature-based solutions to reach $571 billion by 2030 – equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of global gross domestic product.

“But governments cannot do this alone,” he said, calling for the private sector to step up. He pointed to the UN-backed Cali Fund as a mechanism through which companies benefiting from nature can help finance its protection.

Mr. Guterres also cited the rapid growth of renewable energy. The cost of solar power has fallen by almost 90 per cent since 2010 and investment in clean energy is now nearly double investment in fossil fuels. Moreover, renewable energy prevented emissions last year equivalent to the combined emissions of the United States, the European Union and Japan.

“But these benefits are not shared equally around the globe,” he said, noting that many developing countries have been unable to invest sufficiently in both nature and human development due to debt burdens, limited public budgets and an inequitable international financial system.
The Secretary-General’s final appeal was for broad participation, particularly from young people, civil society, women, Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
“Environmental decline often falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and those who did the least to cause the problem. But the solutions often arise from these same groups,” he said.
With 76 days remaining until he leaves office, Mr. Guterres said that confronting climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution had been among his highest priorities.
“Let us act with the urgency this moment demands,” he said. “For our children. For our future. And for all life on Earth.”

articles.title: Ukraine: Civilian casualty rates among ‘deadliest’ in years, as energy attacks intensify

paras.en: Ukraine: Civilian casualty rates among ‘deadliest’ in years, as energy attacks intensify

Civilian casualties in Ukraine remain at record levels, with intensified Russian attacks in September continuing a pattern of harm in 2026 far exceeding previous years, UN human rights monitors in Ukraine said on Friday.
The mission verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September – 85 per cent more than in September 2025.

Casualties were recorded across 22 regions and the city of Kyiv, where civilians were killed or injured on 22 of the month’s 30 days, more often than in any month since the start of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion.
The trend continued into October. On the night of 6 to 7 October alone, a Russian cruise missile and drone attack killed 22 civilians and injured 45 in Pryluky, in Chernihiv region.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the human rights monitoring mission.
The high casualties came as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.

On 13 and 14 October, strikes hit multiple energy facilities, including Kyiv’s three main power stations, temporarily leaving 600,000 people in the capital without electricity, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Ukrainian armed forces also targeted electricity and heating infrastructure in occupied territory and in the Russian Federation, the mission said.
“Systematically attacking electricity and heating infrastructure as winter approaches is bound to inflict significant suffering on the civilian population,” Ms. Bell warned.
Damaged homes and attacks on energy also risk forcing Ukrainians who have returned home to flee again this winter, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) warned.

“For millions of Ukrainians, the challenge is no longer simply whether they can return home. It is whether they can remain there safely and right now the conditions are making it difficult,” said Arthur Erken, IOM Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia.
Some 1.45 million returnees now live in frontline districts, and during the last cold season only 32 per cent of households could heat their homes adequately.
Around 2.1 million older people live alone in apartment buildings, leaving them especially exposed to prolonged power and heating cuts.

Less than seven per cent of IOM’s crisis response plan for Ukraine this year has been funded, Mr. Erken said, calling for urgent support to repair homes, improve insulation and maintain essential services.

Meanwhile, the eighth localised ceasefire brokered by the international nuclear energy watchdog (IAEA) between Ukraine and Russia, began on Thursday to allow repairs to a damaged backup transformer, strengthening the connection between the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant and its sole remaining external power line.
IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi welcomed the cooperation of both sides but warned that diesel fuel at the plant was running low, with no deliveries since March.

“It is essential that steps are taken to increase the volume of diesel fuel available on-site prior to winter, when the situation may become acute,” he said, renewing his call for maximum military restraint from all sides.

articles.title: As disasters mount, next UN climate summit faces a test of trust

paras.en: As disasters mount, next UN climate summit faces a test of trust

Less than a month before the UN climate conference COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, representatives of three successive summit presidencies gathered to address a pressing question: How can the world restore trust in climate action when the consequences of a warming planet are already being felt?
The devastation in Nepal offered a stark reminder of what is at stake.

Opening the high-level meeting at UN Headquarters, General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman evoked the imagery of a wall of water barreling down a mountain valley, sweeping away people, homes and communities in its path.
“Scientists had long warned that such events were becoming a reality, yet none of us were prepared for the shocking footage”.

He reminded delegates that this year's strengthening El Niño could be among the strongest since at least 1950, while the world is on its way to hotting up by 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels under current climate policies, far beyond the Paris Agreement's goals.
“Behind these figures are families uprooted, children's missing, school women walking farther for water, and communities confronting losses they cannot bear,” the assembly president added.
The task ahead for world leaders at the upcoming climate conference COP31 is to then turn commitments into action – and promises into trust, he said.
“COP31 must be more than another negotiating milestone. It must demonstrate that multilateralism delivers.”
Türkiye, which will host the conference from 9 to 20 November, outlined plans to accelerate clean energy, reduce methane emissions and strengthen climate resilience.

Among the key initiatives for this COP is the Climate Implementation Bridge, developed with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), which aims to transform national climate commitments into investment-ready projects and connect them with financing.
“The issue is not simply the overall volume of finance. It is also whether finance is available, accessible, affordable and predictable,” Türkiye's Ambassador to the UN, Ahmet Yıldız said.
For Pacific island nations, the need for action is already immediate.

Rising seas and extreme weather are threatening homes, livelihoods and infrastructure, a reality highlighted by Australia, which is leading the COP31 negotiations under an unprecedented arrangement that sees two countries thousands of miles apart, sharing responsibilities for the climate summit.

“By listening to our most vulnerable communities, partnering with those in need, and accelerating the implementation of practical initiatives, I believe we can restore trust through climate action,” Australian Ambassador James Larsen said.
Mr Larsen called for more accessible climate financing and stronger adaptation plans grounded in science and local needs.
Brazil, which hosted COP30 last year, identified three priorities for Antalya:
- Making the new just transition mechanism operational,
- improving how countries measure progress on adaptation
- expanding climate investment in developing countries struggling with debt

“In a world of States with severe fiscal constraints and high indebtedness, the [finance] talks need to lead to viable solutions for expanding fiscal space for climate investment,” Ambassador Sérgio França Danese urged.
The question of who pays, and who benefits, also runs through Ethiopia’s concerns, which will host COP32.
Africa contributes only around three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, Ambassador Tesfaye Yilma Sabo reminded delegates, yet faces some of the most severe consequences of climate change.
“Delayed action carries a compounding cost for developing countries. The pace of action matters because the gap between current plans and what the science requires remains significant.
Financing and access to technology are increasingly determining who benefits from the transition and who is left behind,” he warned.

World leaders are expected to gather for a special summit in Antalya on 11 and 12 November, with negotiations set to test whether climate commitments can translate into meaningful change for communities most at risk.
But for Mr. Rahman, the measure of success will be found far beyond the negotiating rooms.
“Let COP31 be judged not by promises we repeat, but by the people we protect. That is how we restore trust.”

articles.title: Burnley’s winless run at home to pass one-year mark after Wolves fightback

paras.en: Burnley vs Wolverhampton Wanderers; Sky Bet Championship
Burnley vs Wolverhampton Wanderers. Sky Bet Championship.
Burnley 1-2 Wolves: Fer Lopez on target as Clarets' winless run at Turf Moor extends to 21 league games

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Burnley and Wolves at Turf Moor on Friday; Jamie Vardy scores first goal since returning to English football - but Fer Lopez and Tawanda Chirewa score to ensure Clarets' winless home run goes on
Burnley's run without a home league win will continue beyond the one-year mark after the Clarets were beaten 2-1 by Wolves at Turf Moor.
On October 18, it will be 12 months to the day since they beat Leeds 2-0 in the Premier League.
Since then, they have lost 11 games and drawn the other 10. It is the longest run without a home win across England's top four tiers.

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream EFL games with no contract📺

Jamie Vardy's first English football goal since returning last month put Nicky Hayen's side ahead, but defensive errors allowed Fer Lopez and Tawanda Chirewa to turn the game around, securing Wolves' first win in three and lifting them to sixth.

In an interview with Sky Sports earlier this week, Vardy had been asked if this was his final season as a professional. "We'll have to wait until the summer and let my legs tell my head what they think!" he said.
On Friday night, Vardy proved his legs still have plenty left in them.
The 39-year-old found the net with his second shot of the game, scoring his first goal in English football since May 18, 2025, when he netted his 200th and final goal for Leicester.
But his strike was not enough to send Burnley into half-time ahead. Kyle Walker gifted possession away just outside his own penalty area, and Wolves were quick to punish the costly error.
Sean Neave took over, squaring the ball for Lopez to fire home via the inside of the left-hand post.

Burnley lost their grip on the game after the break and fell behind with 18 minutes remaining. Igor's dreadful touch gifted Chirewa the opportunity to strike, and although his effort was met by Gregoire Coudert's gloves, the ball looped over the goalkeeper and under the crossbar.
Burnley offered little in response and were met with a chorus of boos at the final whistle, as their fifth league defeat of the season was confirmed.

- 7: OVER! Jacob Bruun Larsen drops the ball back to Igor, whose drive dips inches over the crossbar.
- 10: BIG SAVE! Vardy's first shot is kept out by a strong left arm from Jose Sa.
- 20: GOAL! Bruun Larsen plays a lovely ball through for Vardy, who doesn't even look up as he sweeps the ball home.
- 39: GOAL! Against the run of play, Wolves level as Kyle Walker cheaply gives away possession, allowing Sean Neave to square for Fer Lopez to level.
- 52: SAVE! Fer Lopez curls a free-kick around the wall and towards the near post, where Gregoire Coudert is on hand to push it around the post.
- 72: GOAL! Just 21 seconds after coming onto the pitch, Tawanda Chirewa puts Wolves in front for the first time with his first senior club goal.
Hayen: It's difficult to make these mistakes and win
Burnley's Nicky Hayen speaking to Sky Sports:
"A difficult defeat. The first half was actually really good in terms of the organisation. They didn't find a solution, we scored a really good goal and had quite good opportunities.

"Then we give two goals away. You can talk about match plans and tactics, but if we concede two goals like this, by individual mistakes, it's difficult to win games. That's, unfortunately, the reality again.
"They apologised in the dressing room and I accepted it because no one does it on purpose, but it doesn't help us, that's for sure."
On the record at Turf Moor: "We can't talk about the past, but everyone will repeat it. It's normal. We just have to change the mindset because it will change one day."
Wolves' Cesar Peixoto speaking to Sky Sports:
"I'm happy with the performance. I think we deserved to win. We struggled with the press in the first 30 minutes, but after that we managed the game well and created plenty of chances.
"The difference today was our mentality. This was a victory for the whole group and the entire team, especially as almost every player has featured in our last three games.
"It's an important win, but it's only three points."

articles.title: Gloucester claim thrilling draw against Champions Cup holders Bordeaux

paras.en: Champions Cup: Gloucester claim thrilling draw against holders Bordeaux

Will Trenholm scores a brace of tries as Gloucester fall just short of beating Champions Cup holders Bordeaux in a thrilling 36-36 draw; Edinburgh suffered a 27-17 defeat against Toulon in their Challenge Cup opener
Will Trenholm’s brace was not enough to help Gloucester pull off a stunning upset against Champions Cup holders Bordeaux, as they were forced to settle for a 36-36 draw after a dramatic contest.
George Skivington's team pushed the French outfit all the way during a pulsating European tie at Kingsholm Stadium.
Gloucester held a 24-17 lead at half-time before Trenholm crashed over twice, but a double by Louis Bielle-Biarrey salvaged a share of the spoils for visiting Bordeaux.

Bordeaux made a fast start, with Martin Page-Relo able to open the scoring in the fourth minute, but Arthur Clark produced an instant reply for Gloucester.
Efforts by Max Llewellyn and George Barton, either side of Sipili Falatea's try, earned the hosts a slender seven-point advantage at the break thanks to three successful conversions by Barton.

Pablo Uberti levelled for Bordeaux six minutes into the second period before quick-fire tries by Trenholm had Kingsholm rocking, but Bielle-Biarry levelled in the 62nd minute and despite plenty of territory, neither side could find a winning score.
Edinburgh beaten by Toulon in Challenge Cup opener
Edinburgh suffered a 27-17 defeat against Toulon in their Challenge Cup opener as Malvyn Jaminet scored 22 points for the French visitors.
Defences were on top in the first half at the Hive Stadium, with two Jaminet penalties to one from James Grayson giving Toulon a 6-3 lead at the break.
Jaminet extended that advantage three minutes into the second half, collecting his own kick before converting his try.
Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman hit back immediately for Edinburgh, with Grayson adding the conversion, but Fiji international Seta Tuicuvu soon barged over and Jaminet again added the extras.
Edinburgh refused to go away, with replacement Geordie Gwynn scoring with his first touch before Grayson converted to keep the hosts in contention.

But Toulon had the final say. Baptiste Serin set up Jaminet for another converted try, while Piers O'Conor's yellow card for direct contact with Jeremy Sinzelle's head compounded Edinburgh's misery and sealed their fate.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink, disrupting military amid Trump pressure
articles.author: Jane Lytvynenko

paras.en: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of undermining its ability to defend itself by limiting Starlink internet services as it reeled from intense Russian ballistic missile attacks that it said came without the usual warning from allies.

Musk put the responsibility for the restrictions on President Donald Trump’s shoulders on social media, saying the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is owned and controlled by the U.S. government.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said.
A spokesperson for President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC News that the limitations remained in place late Wednesday.

Facing pressure from Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried that Washington could cut off battlefield support to try to force it into concessions at the negotiating table.

Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence-sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News.

Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intelligence, but with relations spiraling, Ukrainian officials and military units accused SpaceX on Wednesday of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations.
It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally.
The Ukrainian government has yet to receive a response from SpaceX, a Ukrainian official told NBC News, and Ukrainian units are already reporting issues with performance even at lower UAV speeds.

Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said Starshield is lifesaving. “The technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destructions in Ukraine caused by Russian side,” he said.
SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov.

“Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added.
An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations.

The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control.
“The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement.
Beskrestnov said restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph.

Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses, as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he said. Asked about the importance of the technology, Sienik said, “The technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.”
Ukraine has reached out to the U.S. government and SpaceX for clarification about the rationale for the new restrictions but has yet to receive a response, according to a Ukrainian official.
Ukraine’s armed forces learned about the limitations from customer support after they filed a complaint about operational issues, the official said, adding that SpaceX had not warned of the move.
Ukrainian military units were already reporting issues with drone performance at even lower speeds, the official added.
The White House, SpaceX and Starlink did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The disruption follows days of mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington as Trump pushes to lower gas prices ahead of the midterm elections. Trump’s latest reversal in his bid to settle the war led him to stun Kyiv by striking a diesel deal with Russia that upended years of U.S. sanctions.

He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. Trump also announced an “energy ceasefire” that neither warring side appears to have agreed to.

Kyiv said it had refrained from striking Russian energy targets to respect Trump’s wishes, but the Kremlin has continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in its annual effort to leave its neighbor in the freezing dark as winter sets in.

Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had not received any early warning from its partners about “a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv” a day earlier. Explosions rang out before an alert was issued, according to an NBC News producer in the capital.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues,” Zelenskyy said, without singling out the U.S.
Later Tuesday, he reported that another strike on Kyiv was “the second time Ukraine was not warned.”

Since Russia invaded Ukraine more than four years ago, the U.S. has provided significant satellite and eavesdropping intelligence to Kyiv. European partners also share intelligence with Kyiv, but Ukrainian officials see the U.S. intelligence assistance as crucial to their fight against Russia.
Trump denied withholding information critical to Ukraine’s defense, despite reported threats to cut off U.S. intelligence if Kyiv failed to stop its attacks on Russian refineries.
“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he told reporters Tuesday.

After the first Russian attack Monday, when five ballistic missiles were able to strike civilian infrastructure without notice from the U.S., two Ukrainian officials told NBC News it was the result of a technical issue, or glitch, in U.S. intelligence-sharing.

Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha reassured the audience that U.S. intelligence-sharing continued, blaming the delayed alert on a “special type of the weaponry” used by Russia.
But after the second attack Tuesday, Ukrainian and European officials said the reason was less clear.
“We didn’t receive warning for a second time, and this doesn’t look like a coincidence,” one of the Ukrainian officials said.
The second Ukrainian official attributed the issue to bad weather. Two European officials told NBC News they were still trying to understand why there was no notice.

The Ukrainian air force spokesman, Col. Yurii Ihnat, said Wednesday that after the second ballistic strike on Kyiv without a warning, “in the next three waves of attacks, notifications from partners about the use of ballistic weapons did come through.”
Later, Zelenskyy acknowledged that he felt betrayed by what was happening with the U.S.
But the situation went beyond his emotions, Zelenskyy said in an interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored.”
“It’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” he said. “I mean, our country has to survive.”
“It’s a pity that we are losing strong partner,” he added, referring to the U.S.
The Kremlin noted the confusion Wednesday but said it was “too early to draw any systemic conclusions.”

Zelenskyy said at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were without power Wednesday after the latest wave of Russian attacks, adding that President Vladimir Putin was in clear violation of the energy truce announced by Trump. “Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he added.
Like Trump, Musk has repeatedly oscillated in his stance on the war.
He turned on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
It has become a lifeline for war-torn parts of the country, but it has also facilitated battlefield communications and enabled the use of longer-range drones, given its resistance to signal jamming.
Musk agreed to turn off thousands of Russian-used Starlinks in Ukraine this year, causing problems for the Kremlin’s forces. But in recent days, he has echoed Trump’s criticism.

articles.title: Tech stocks erase $1 trillion of wealth as oil surges to $110 for the first time since May
articles.author: Steve Kopack

paras.en: Tech stocks shed more than $1 trillion in value Friday, as the price of oil soared to its highest levels in five months.

The Nasdaq 100 index, which tracks most of the country’s largest tech and AI-linked companies, sold off by 2.5% and now sits about 7% below its most recent all-time high — a record it had only notched last week.
The S&P 500 dropped 1% and the Russell 2000 index fell 1.6%. The Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped 3.8% for its eight straight day of losses, the longest such streak since 2008.
The sharp drop in tech shares came as worries about ballooning debt, high interest rates and rising oil prices all resurfaced.

Brent crude oil, widely considered to be among the most important prices in global energy, surpassed $110 per barrel shortly after 2:30 p.m. ET, its highest level since May. It ended the week at $109.86 per barrel, still its highest closing level since May 19.

U.S. crude oil, which also steers gas prices, jumped 3.5% Friday to close at $101.41 per barrel. It was the first time West Texas Intermediate crude had crossed the $100 threshold, closely watched by both traders and the public, since September.

The continued upward trend in energy prices increases the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this year. The Fed already boosted rates by 0.25% in September to tame inflation that had risen as a result of higher oil and gas prices.
Diesel futures also jumped Friday by more than 1%. The cost of this commercial fuel critical for farming and other industrial sectors has risen even faster than regular gasoline in recent months.
The steady rise in the price of fuel around the world began this spring, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February and triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
But an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months has caused an even more dramatic price spike for diesel.
Russia has traditionally been one of the world’s largest diesel exporters. But attacks by Ukrainian forces on its energy infrastructure has taken much of its refining capacity offline.
On Friday, another Russian refiner suspended some crude oil operations. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”
Energy assets in Ukraine have also been targeted by Russian strikes.

As the world seeks alternative sources for diesel, there are few clear opportunities to expand diesel production. Refineries in the U.S. and Europe are already running at nearly maximum capacity to churn out as much diesel fuel as possible.
President Donald Trump is intensely focused on the high cost of diesel fuel because of its key role in driving up inflation — a top issue for American voters in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Trump has tried multiple actions to lower prices, but those have not resulted in a significant step-down for diesel prices.

The president has also touted a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin as a way to lower prices, but as of Friday, no actual Russian diesel had been identified as having reached the global market.
Additionally, a group of American lawmakers introduced a bill that would block Trump’s Russian diesel deal. It has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House.

But polling indicates that Republicans are unlikely to maintain a majority in the House after November’s elections. The Russian diesel-blocking bill offers a preview of the kind of legislation that could advance under Democratic control.
Yet even now, the legislation adds to “growing doubts that a U.S.-Russia diesel deal will come to fruition,” said Mason Mendez, global real assets analyst at Wells Fargo.
“Investors also remain concerned about further military escalation in the Middle East, as attacks on commercial shipping and regional infrastructure have increased in recent weeks,” he said.
“Looking into 2027, the need to rebuild depleted global inventories could create an additional source of demand and keep energy prices elevated for longer.”

At the same time that inflation pushes interest rates higher around the world, trillion-dollar tech companies are borrowing and spending hundreds of billions of dollars to develop AI and build their vast data centers.
This week, fresh cracks began to show in the AI business model, as investors raised questions about when their massive injections of cash into AI companies would pay off.
The two worst performing stocks in the Nasdaq 100 on Friday were both data center companies: Nebuius and CoreWeave.
The value of CoreWeave’s shares has plunged more than 25% over the past month.
But these companies are just two of the dozens that have borrowed billions of dollars at high interest rates to expand at a breakneck pace.

Just a day before Friday’s sell-off, Ed Yardeni, a highly regarded market analyst, cut his year-end S&P 500 target to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates.
