paras.en: Asked about reports that private traders in Gaza had halted cooperation with the Israeli authorities on allowing commercial trucks carrying food to enter the occupied enclave, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed that the uninterrupted flow of “humanitarian and commercial goods” remained essential, “so children can continue their recovery”.
He recalled being in Gaza City last year before the ceasefire began, when supplies “were not getting in” and famine was declared by UN-backed food insecurity experts.

“We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he insisted, “where children are not receiving what they need to survive and to continue to have hope for their future”.

The UNICEF alert comes as temperatures drop and displaced families in Gaza fill empty flour bags with sand to keep rainwater out of their tents. Aid agencies continue to repeat warnings that the situation in Gaza remains dire, after three years of war, sparked by Hamas-led terror attacks in Israel.
The ongoing sanitation crisis is a particular concern in the war-torn enclave, where Israeli bombardment has severely damaged the drainage network.

“There are vast pools of wastewater, such as the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin that is half-full,” Mr. Pires warned. “With the winter rains fast approaching, we’re running out of time to pump this out. Just as we warned a year ago, contaminated water could overflow and inundate downstream residential areas with potentially life-threatening impacts for children and their families. Children have drowned in sewage-contaminated water before.”

According to UNICEF, 800,000 children remain displaced in Gaza “and most live in tents or dangerous bombed-out buildings”. An estimated 60,000 children have seen either one or both parents killed during the war, or since the ceasefire, while nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover.
As part of UN assistance to Palestinians in Gaza, UNICEF has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including at over 200 UNICEF-supported learning centres.
The agency has also provided digital cash assistance – “a lifeline”, Mr. Pires stressed – to more than 380,000 people, along with safe water to 1.2 million people.

articles.title: WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents

paras.en: WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents

The UN agency’s eastern Mediterranean region comprises 22 countries and territories. Intensified support is being given to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, which have been identified as priority countries.
This follows deadly outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in both the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda and confirmation of a case in Kenya linked to the DRC.
Hostilities and overstretched health systems

Although there have not been any Ebola cases in the region so far, conflict, displacement and overstretched health systems in several countries are making it difficult to prepare and respond should the situation change.
In a speech earlier this week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Gebreyesus described the region as “the epicentre of global humanitarian need”.
More than 117 million people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Sudan, Syria, Yemen and beyond, require humanitarian assistance to survive.
Assessing readiness, identifying challenges

Between July and September, WHO deployed missions to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan to assess national readiness and identify challenges in Ebola surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination.
The UN agency is helping authorities to address gaps through training, technical support, medical supplies and simulation exercises.

It has developed regional readiness checklists, contingency planning tools and technical guidance, in addition to strengthening coordination with countries in both Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean.
WHO has also provided laboratory supplies, traveller guidance and community engagement resources.
Despite progress, gaps remain in early detection, laboratory confirmation and availability of protective equipment and resources for emergency response.
“Conflict, insecurity and restricted access present additional challenges, particularly in countries already facing major humanitarian emergencies,” WHO said.
Meanwhile, work continues to ensure that national authorities and partners can rapidly detect, investigate and manage suspected Ebola cases.

articles.title: The All Blacks' Haka explained - plus rugby's other rituals

paras.en: New Zealand's Haka explained - meaning and origin of All Blacks' rugby war dance plus Cibi, Siva Tau, Sipi Tau rituals

We look at history of New Zealand's haka in rugby union; the most memorable haka responses over the decades; and at Fiji's Cibi, Samoa's Siva Tau, Tonga's Sipi Tau; Watch All Blacks face Australia in Sydney on Saturday October 17 (6am) live on Sky Sports Main Event
One of the most intriguing and anticipated moments in the sport of rugby union: the sight of New Zealand's All Blacks performing their world-famous haka as the opposition stands before them.
But how much do you know about the haka? And also of the three other ceremonial war dances which take place in rugby: the Cibi, Siva Tau and Sipi Tau.
Find out everything you need to know below...
History of the haka in sport - When did it start? What does it mean?

An ancient traditional Māori practice, there is no single recorded date for the haka's first-ever performance owing to this very reason. It has been practised by indigenous Māori communities for centuries.
The earliest point at which Europeans witnessed the haka was the 18th century: Joseph Banks and James Cook on their first voyage to New Zealand in 1769 recorded the haka as "vigorous and ferocious".

In terms of its introduction into sport, New Zealand's first rugby union side visited Australia in Sydney in 1884 and performed the haka. During 1888/89, a 'New Zealand native team' toured the UK for the first time, performing the haka on October 3 1888 against Surrey in a tour match.
The year 1905 saw the birth of the 'All Blacks' as they toured Britain with a team which came to be known as 'The Originals.'
The All Blacks performed their famous "Ka Mate" haka before Tests against Scotland and Wales, with it having been composed in 1820 by Māori chief Te Rauparaha.
Yet, the tradition of the All Blacks performing the haka on home soil and before every Test they played did not become custom until 1986.
Ahead of rugby's first World Cup in 1987, All Black Buck Shelford set about reforming the haka in order for pre-match performances to be organised, in sync and executed properly.

"If we're going to do it, we're going to do it right. Either perform the haka properly or not at all. Vote on it and decide which way you want to go," Shelford is said to have told team-mates at the time.
Shelford and team-mate Hika Reid subsequently taught and trained the All Blacks squad correct pronunciation of words and actions, and of the haka's importance.
At the 1987 World Cup in New Zealand, with Shelford now captain, the All Blacks performed the haka in New Zealand for the very first time, en route to the All Blacks clinching the trophy.
In terms of what the haka means, "Ka Mate" is the recitation of a traditional Māori poem about life, death and resilience.
The more common haka performed by the All Blacks today is the 'Kapa o Pango', first performed in August 2005 before a Tri-Nations Test against South Africa in Dunedin.
The haka featured an extended and aggressive introduction by team captain Tana Umaga, highlighted by a drawing of the thumb down the throat.
Famous haka responses - how should teams respond?
There have been a number of famous haka responses from opposition sides over the years.

In 1996, Australia famously (or infamously?) decided to totally ignore the haka altogether in Wellington, turning their backs on the All Blacks, following on from Wallabies great David Campese choosing to ignore the haka and do kicking drills ahead of the 1991 Rugby World Cup semi-final between the sides, which Australia won.

In 2019, England adopted a V-shaped formation in Yokohama ahead of their World Cup semi-final against the All Blacks. Once the haka started, English players progressed beyond the halfway line and held their ground as officials tried to move them.

England were later fined £2000 by World Rugby for breaching World Cup 2019 rules relating to cultural challenges, which stated no players from the team receiving the challenge may advance beyond the halfway line. England won the match 19-7 after a sensational performance.

At the 2007 World Cup, France faced the All Blacks in a World Cup quarter-final in Cardiff, and memorably walked up in a line of opposition to the All Blacks, coming within a metre of the haka. France won the match 20-18.
France also marched forward in an arrow-formation facing the haka ahead of the 2011 Rugby World Cup final in New Zealand, before controversially losing 8-7 at Eden Park.

In 2005, the All Blacks agreed to a request from the Welsh Rugby Union to repeat the sequence of events from the original match a century before in 1905, which involved the haka taking place after the New Zealand national anthem but before the Welsh one.

A year later in 2006, Wales demanded a repeat of the sequence, which the All Blacks refused, ultimately performing the haka in the dressing rooms and not in front of the watching fans. Then All Blacks captain Richie McCaw defended the decision by stating the haka was "integral to New Zealand culture and the All Blacks' heritage" and "if the other team wants to mess around, we'll just do the haka in the shed."

Two years later in 2008, another memorable Wales vs New Zealand haka situation unfolded, as following the conclusion of the haka in Cardiff, Wales refused to break and move until the All Blacks did. Neither side did for nearly a minute-and-a-half despite urging from referee Jonathan Kaplan, until McCaw instructed the All Blacks to break off. Wales led 9-6 at half-time but were eventually well beaten 29-9.

In 2016, Ireland faced the All Blacks in Chicago seeking a first-ever win over New Zealand in 111 years. Just weeks prior, Munster coach Anthony Foley had died in his sleep in Paris at the age of 42 ahead of a European Cup contest against Racing 92.

Facing the haka, Ireland lined up in a figure of eight in memory of Foley, a former Ireland and Munster No 8 in his playing days. Ireland went on to clinch a stunning 40-29 maiden win over the All Blacks.
Before their 2023 Rugby World Cup quarter-final, Ireland repeated the same haka response, but lost to the All Blacks in Paris 28-24.

In 2008, a uniquely stirring haka response took place at Thomond Park in Limerick as Munster quartet Doug Howlett, Rua Tipoki, Lifeimi Mafi and Jeremy Manning stepped forward to perform a haka facing the All Blacks with the rest of their Munster team-mates stood behind them.

A similar event took place recently in 2026 when All Blacks great Ma'a Nonu performed a solo haka facing the All Blacks while a player for South African club side the Sharks, ahead of New Zealand's tour match in Durban.
Are New Zealand only nation that perform the haka?
While the haka is rugby's best-known and most famous traditional pre-match ceremonial war dance, the island nations of Fiji, Samoa and Tonga all also perform their own versions.

Fiji perform the Cibi, which sees the team stand in formation and led by a vocal soloist, before dropping into a synchronised low crouch or knee-bend while making aggressive arm and hand gestures, concluding with an explosive jump or step-up.

Samoa perform the Siva Tau, with the ritual led by a designated chanter and players starting in a lowered or kneeling stance before rising into synchronised movements that include chest-slapping, foot-stomping, aggressive gestures, and intense vocal chanting.

Tonga perform the Sipi Tau, which begins with the team huddled or kneeling in a circle led by a central caller, before breaking into a structured formation on the field featuring deep squats, chest-pounding, rhythmic foot-stomping, and aggressive synchronised gestures.

articles.title: McIlroy plays just four holes of second round due to bad light in India

paras.en: DP World India Championship: Rory McIlroy four off clubhouse lead but through only four holes of second round

Bad light halts play on day two in New Delhi with Rory McIlroy through only four holes of his second round, having eagled the first; Joost Luiten, Angel Hidalgo and Adrian Meronk share clubhouse lead on eight under; watch DP World India Championship on Sky Sports Golf
Rory McIlroy is four shots off the clubhouse lead but only four holes into his second round at the DP World India Championship after play was suspended early on Friday due to bad light in New Delhi.

Torrential rain on the Thursday resulted in a five-hour delay to the opening round, and there were further frustrations for those still out on the course when play was halted just before 6pm local time on Friday.
The second round is scheduled to restart at 6.45am on Saturday.

McIlroy, who is bidding to win the Race to Dubai title for a record-equalling eighth time, opened the tournament with a two-under 70 on Thursday, while he started his second round with an eagle to sit four under when play was stopped shortly after.

Dutchman Joost Luiten, who had to play 34 holes on Friday because of the delays, Angel Hidalgo and Alfred Dunhill Links Championship winner Adrian Meronk were all able to finish their second rounds, and top the leaderboard on eight under.
Belgian Thomas Detry is also eight under, but is only through six holes of his second round, for which he is currently three under.
England's Eddie Pepperell, who hit a six-under 66, and Todd Clements are both one shot back having also got into the clubhouse before the light faded.
Eugenio Chacarra is another at seven under, through five holes, as he looks for a strong finish to push his own challenge in the Race to Dubai rankings, currently sitting second.
Scotland's Robert MacIntyre was level par through five holes, also at four under overall, alongside defending champion Tommy Fleetwood, who was two under after four.
McIlroy was third in the DP World Tour standings coming into this penultimate event before the play-offs.
Leader Patrick Reed got through his second round at three under, recovering from a double-bogey at the fourth, but is level par overall.

United States GP track - Circuit of the Americas

articles.title: Kevin Warsh says Fed is focused on taming rising prices, but gives no hint about next rate hike
articles.author: Steve Kopack

paras.en: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Friday said that the U.S. economy has “broadly” moved in the direction that the central bank expected during its last meeting in September, when it raised rates for the first time since 2023.

In the weeks since, inflation as measured by the consumer price index jumped to 3.7%. For businesses, inflation has hit even harder. That turned investors focus to Warsh’s appearance at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for a signal about whether the Fed would hike rates in October or December.

“We made very clear we’d deliver price stability,” Warsh said Friday morning in Bangkok (Thursday night ET), a signal of his focus on inflation and that another interest rate hike is likely on the horizon.
But Warsh stuck to a familiar tone and refused to give any clear hint about how soon that might come. “We’re not in that business anymore,” he said.
However, Warsh, the head of the world’s most important central bank, spoke at length about one major economic force that is causing prices to rise across the economy.
“In the United States, we’re having a massive investment surge,” he said, referencing the seemingly ever-expanding AI boom.
“It’s probably the most important thing that’s happening in the global economy on the upside,” Warsh said. “I think it’s going to fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy.”
A central feature of the AI boom is an expansive buildout of data centers around the country.

To fund all that building, trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components. Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices for consumers as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.
Warsh said AI could also “change the real economy,” though he acknowledged not knowing how deeply it would impact employment.

But he projected optimism about the technology’s prospects, predicting that “it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive.” He said it should also generate “more wealth.”
“But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one,” he warned.
Warsh said a Fed task force of outside experts studying the impact of AI on the labor market would hold a public hearing on the topic in November.

“So I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose to the day jobs that you and I have,” Warsh remarked. “I think it’s an exciting development and it’s an innovation that I think a decade from now they’ll look back on and they’ll say this was hugely consequential.”

His comments will be closely scrutinized because they are the last from any Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.
Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.
But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.
Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”
“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.
“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”
Despite the challenges facing the U.S. economy, Warsh concluded on an optimistic note, saying that those should strengthen it in the long run.

“What is striking to me are two things: almost everywhere in the global economy showing resilience that I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what’s happening in geopolitics and hot spots around the world.”

Warsh added, “I believe, optimistically, you might think naively, at least in the U.S. we’re going to come out of this stronger, with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.”

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil sites is a ‘disgrace’
articles.author: Yuliya Talmazan

paras.en: President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections.

Kyiv said Thursday that it would no longer abide by Trump’s “energy ceasefire,” citing Russia’s refusal to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the U.S. of costing civilian lives by striking deals with Moscow and withdrawing support that is crucial to Kyiv’s defense against the invasion launched by President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian officials had raised alarm after gaps in intelligence sharing left Kyiv vulnerable to Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink satellite service disrupted military operations. Zelenskyy said Friday that the technology was still not fully restored.
With Ukraine defying his demands to halt strikes, Trump responded late Thursday.

“If you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. “I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets; they don’t have to hit,” Trump said.

“Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with” on the war, he said, adding that “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
As his clash escalated with Trump, Zelenskyy was in Brussels on Friday to shore up support from European allies, whom he called “real leaders” as they gathered for a crucial summit.

Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery Thursday after Zelenskyy said he was “done” with the truce, which Trump had announced to the apparent surprise of both sides in the war. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv reported any new strikes on Russian refineries Friday.
Trump has sought to blame Ukraine’s strikes for destabilizing the price of diesel globally, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
But this campaign of attacks deep inside enemy territory has given Ukraine crucial leverage, sparking a major fuel crisis inside Russia.

Kyiv hoped this would give it a stronger hand at the negotiating table, but as Washington pushes for an end to the conflict it has taken a series of steps that have caused surprise and alarm among Ukraine and its backers in Europe.

Last week, Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Russia, an apparent attempt to relieve pressure at the pump for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections but which reversed years of U.S. policy. Trump then called for Kyiv to stop all strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and said Zelenskyy had to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader.

It comes amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. is still sharing critical military intelligence with Ukraine after a pair of major strikes earlier this week that Kyiv said came without a usual advance warning from its partners.
Ukraine also reported a slowing down of the Starlink satellite terminals, which are critical for its army’s communications, drone missions and aerial defenses.
Kyiv said that Starshield, the military version of the technology that is used by Ukraine’s troops, had been limited without any warning.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk, the billionaire Trump ally, said that such decisions were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.

After repeated requests for comment about Musk’s statement, a senior U.S. official told NBC News that “no such request was ever made by the president.” Trump has also denied restricting military intelligence for Ukraine.

Kyiv said Thursday the Starshield service was being restored, but the episode only added to the mounting suspicion in Ukraine that the U.S. was willing to cut it off from battlefield support in order to exert pressure for a peace deal. Asked about the service on Friday, Zelenskyy said that issues were ongoing. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was? No. Is the speed returning? Yes,” he told reporters in Brussels.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid the stalemate in peace talks.
The Kremlin agreed with Trump on Friday, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was clear that “Zelenskyy doesn’t want to take responsibility and move toward a peaceful resolution.”
Russia has always stated it’s open to a peace settlement but only on its own hard-line terms, which would see Ukraine ceding significant territory.

articles.title: At least three killed by Russian drones in Ukraine which cut power to 370,000

paras.en: At least three people were killed by Russian drones in Ukraine overnight, the strikes also cut power to around 370,000 people.
Russia appears eager to publicise a Ukrainian strike on a an oil refinery, after Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire.
EU Leaders rallied around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Brussels, extending support to cover Ukraine's budget gap.
At least three people have been killed by Russian drones in Ukraine, with strikes also hitting two shopping centres and key energy grid infrastructure.
Two people died and 12 more were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.
In the north-western region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk.
The attacks on Ukranian energy grids cut power to around 370,000 in the north-west after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.
Crews set out to repair damage to the grid in Volyn and had reconnected about 100,000 people by later in the morning, Mr Romaniuk added.
The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn's regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.
Other attacks hit at least two shopping centre, one in the northern city of Sumy, which sits close to the front line, and one in the neighbouring region of Rivne, officials said.
The strikes in Sumy were the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.
Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping centre and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.

Russia publicly acknowledged a Ukrainian drone strike on a major oil refinery this week and broadcast images on state media, breaking its usual practice in order to highlight the attack that US President Donald Trump branded a "disgrace".
Ukraine has frequently struck Russian oil refineries in attacks that officials typically describe as hits on "industrial enterprises".
The target of Thursday's attack in Ryazan was immediately identified by the regional governor as one of Russia's largest refineries.
For the first time since the start of the war, state TV showed the aftermath of the Ryazan refinery attack.
In a brief report, the Rossiya-24 channel showed the plant with a relatively small plume of black smoke rising from the sit, no fire was visible.
Russia is eager to publicise the incident, which took place four days after Mr Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, which neither side confirmed they had agreed to.
Ukraine said it paused such attacks for three days in deference to Mr Trump, but resumed because Russia had continued to pound its thermal power plants and other energy infrastructure.
European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Brussels on Friday.

The support is off the back of Mr Trumps remarks on Ukraine's strikes on Russia, a recent diesel deal signed between Russia and the US, and allegations the US is withholding critical intelligence from Ukraine.

"We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That's why we have to prepare for the winter," Mr Zelenskyy said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defence and funding."
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
"Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell," he said.
"We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs. Because always, at the start [and] at the end of every conversation.
"People need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting … for us."

articles.title: A rugby union player has died the day before championship competition begins

paras.en: Professional athlete dies day before a game, after suffering cardiac arrest in France
A South African rugby union player has died in France.
He reportedly suffered a cardiac arrest and was found unconscious in a hotel shower.
Team officials are working to notify the player's family.

articles.title: Violent clashes involving slingshots during West Bank olive harvest
articles.author: Matthew Doran

paras.en: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and journalists in the occupied West Bank with slingshots and rocks.
The violent attacks happened during the yearly olive harvest.
The Israeli Defense Force says it is examine "all circumstances surrounding the incident".
Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and journalists in the occupied West Bank, using slingshots to hurl rocks from hilltops around the village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.
The violent attacks happened during the yearly olive harvest, which is regularly a flashpoint between the settlers and Palestinians who rely on the crop as a source of income.
Some of the settlers set fire to the olive trees, sending smoke billowing across the area.
Veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was among those attacked, despite wearing a flak jacket emblazoned with the word "press".

She was beaten by settlers, who stole her camera and phone, before being taken to hospital in Ramallah after other journalists rushed to her aid once the settlers had pulled briefly back from the area.
"We saw in the distance in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men," Ms Levine told journalists in hospital, fighting back tears.
"I had a 500 millimetre lens that you could see the mask with slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground.
"Luckily, I had my flak jacket and my helmet. Otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here because they just kept kicking me, and kicking me in, like, probably 50 times."
Ms Levine questioned the parents of the violent settlers, many of whom are often teenage boys or young men.
"I don't know how a parent can raise such monsters," she said.
"They are giving everyone in the country a horrible reputation.
"And unfortunately, everyone is seeing them who they are. And you know what? Sadly, none of them will be prosecuted. I am sure of it."
Israel investigating incident in West Bank
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said his country condemned violence against anyone, but said the circumstances around the attacks in Abu Falah "remain unclear".
In a statement posted on X, it said "serious questions remain" and suggested 200 Palestinians had "confronted" around 40 settlers, and that people on "both sides" were "hurling objects".
"We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonise the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria," Mr Netanyahu's office said.
"The facts must determine the conclusions. Not the headlines."
Witnesses reported seeing soldiers from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), who were called to the area, fire tear gas at Palestinians in the area.
The IDF said it would examine "all circumstances surrounding the incident".
"Upon arriving at the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said.

"At another location where the confrontation took place, IDF soldiers fired warning shots into the air and subsequently toward a suspect who ran toward them carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them.
"The IDF strongly condemns this incident and views any manifestation of violence with utmost severity. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area."
Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray issued a note to staff about the attack.

"While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

"The safety of our journalists is of paramount importance for The Post, as is the right of journalists everywhere to report freely and the responsibility of authorities to protect journalists doing their work.
"We will press for an investigation and support Heidi in the wake of this shocking attack."
It came a week after settlers attacked a photographer from AFP in the West Bank.

While attacks by settlers on foreigners, particularly journalists, often get attention due to the fact they happen with media witnesses, Palestinians argue they bear the brunt of the violence on a daily basis.

Humanitarian organisations, including the United Nations, have reported a surge in settler violence since October 2023, emboldened by the decisions and policies of the right-wing Netanyahu Government which includes settlers in its ministerial ranks.
Israeli organisation Yesh Din said there had been 170 attacks since late September when the olive harvest began.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned settler violence in the West Bank, but has also tried to diminish the significance of it by repeatedly claiming it is just a handful of individuals breaking the law.
The IDF and Israel Police are regularly criticised for failing to prosecute settlers for their offences, while insisting they are taking a firm stance against criminals.
At least half a million Israelis live in settlements scattered across the occupied West Bank.
Their presence is considered illegal under international law.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, American journalist during West Bank olive harvest
articles.author: Jillian Kestler-D'Amours

paras.en: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, American journalist during West Bank olive harvest
Israeli army says incident in Abu Falah 'will be examined'

Dozens of masked Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and injured an American journalist during olive harvesting in the occupied West Bank, according to witnesses and video footage from the incident.
About 80 settlers descended from a hill toward Palestinians who were collecting olives on Friday in Abu Falah, a Palestinian village about 25 kilometres northeast of Ramallah, Reuters reported.
Videos from the scene showed some of the settlers using slingshots to launch stones toward the Palestinians. Photos also showed olive trees burning next to a large group of settlers.
Reuters said at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area partway through the attack, which continued after the army's arrival.
Israeli soldiers also fired tear gas in the direction of Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps, the news agency added. Some Palestinians threw stones to defend themselves during the attack.
An Israeli settler casts a projectile toward Palestinians in Abu Falah. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

Caught up in the attack was Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was reporting in the village when Israeli settlers assaulted her, the U.S. newspaper said. The Post reported she was knocked to the ground, repeatedly kicked and stripped of her cameras and phone.
Video footage showed Levine — who was wearing a helmet and vest marked "press" — lying on her side on a dirt path, with her hands over her face as at least three settlers surrounded her.
"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist," Matt Murray, the Post's executive director, said in a written statement Friday morning.

"While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."
Speaking to reporters from a Ramallah hospital bed, a visibly shaken Levine said she was "brutally attacked."
"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and my helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me," she said.
Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine says Israeli settlers 'kept kicking and kicking' her during the attack in Abu Falah. (Ali Sawafta/Reuters)
'Incident will be examined,' Israeli army says
The Israeli military said in a written statement on social media that troops and Israel Border Police were dispatched to an area near Abu Falah "following a report of a violent confrontation."
"All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the army said.

It also said that at another location where confrontations were taking place, soldiers fired "toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them." The statement didn't provide additional information about that suspect.
"Violence against innocent civilians is a grave and intolerable phenomenon that requires a co-ordinated, multi-agency response," it said, adding that it would work "to eradicate this phenomenon."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the incident was under investigation and that "those responsible will be held accountable." It also stressed that the investigation "must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence."

The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media working in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories, condemned the incident as "the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians" in the West Bank.
"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it said.
Palestinians and an Israeli military vehicle are seen near a fire in the West Bank village of Abu Falah on Friday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Friday's incident comes amid escalating Israeli settler violence against Palestinians across the West Bank.

Earlier this week, the United Nations humanitarian office (OCHA) said nearly 200 settler attacks linked to this year's olive harvest — an annual event that holds historical and cultural significance for Palestinians — have led to casualties or property damage so far.
"That is more than the 185 incidents recorded during the entire 2025 season," it said.

Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, which states that an occupying power cannot transfer its civilian population into the territory that it occupies.
Palestinians walk in Abu Falah after the olive harvest was disrupted by an Israeli settler attack on Friday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Israel rejects that, calling the areas "disputed," and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of the settlements.

In late September, Netanyahu condemned "violent riots" by settlers after a wave of attacks on Palestinians in the village of Qusra. "The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public," he said in a written statement.
Human rights groups have accused the Israeli government of facilitating settler violence as part of an effort to displace Palestinians.

articles.title: See the Amazon rainforest wildfires that have politicians pointing fingers amid Brazil presidential elections

paras.en: See the Amazon rainforest wildfires that have politicians pointing fingers amid Brazil presidential elections
Fires a point of contention during election campaign that has rarely touched on climate change

Brazilian authorities are investigating whether a recent surge in wildfires in the Amazon rainforest have been set on purpose for political motives ahead of the second round of presidential elections later this months.

Fire counts across the biome, which have been near historic lows this year, have tripled since Oct. 4, when Brazilians voted in the first round of national elections. Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, won 47 per cent of the vote, while President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva received 45 per cent. The two will face off in an Oct. 25 runoff.
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after voting in Rio de Janeiro on Oct. 4. (Lucas Landau/The Associated Press)
"The indications are that there has been a premeditated effort" to start the fires, Environment Minister João Paulo Capobianco told The Associated Press.

Capobianco and environmental enforcement officials flew over burned areas on Sunday and again on Wednesday. He said they observed fires in protected forest areas arranged in a distinct geometric pattern, suggesting they may have been deliberately set.

It's not clear who might have started the fires or what their motivations may be. The wildfires have particularly hit Amazonas and Para states over the past few days. Smoke has disrupted daily life in Manaus, the capital of Amazonas and the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon. Public school classes were cancelled and residents were urged to wear face masks.
A resident with a flashlight looks at wildfires burning in Autazes, Brazil, on Oct. 12. (Edmar Barros/The Associated Press)
Local politicians have claimed credit for firefighting efforts or accused authorities of failing to act.
The fires have also become a point of contention outside the Amazon, in an election campaign in which forest protection and climate change have received little attention.

Deforestation in the Amazon soared under former president Bolsonaro, while Lula has brought it back down to the lowest in a decade. Flavio Bolsonaro has denied climate change but said he is an environmental defender, without offering details on protecting the Amazon or supporting forest financing. In speeches, he has called for modernizing environmental laws, which many environmentalists read as loosening them.
A sunset is visible through smoke near the city of Autazes, Brazil, on Oct. 9. (Michael Dantas/AFP/Getty)

The Bolsonaros' most popular allies — Nikolas Ferreira, a lawmaker from the state of Minas Gerais, and re-elected Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcísio de Freitas, both from southeastern Brazil — cited wildfires last week to criticize Lula's government. De Freitas said Lula's Workers Party were hypocrites and "disappeared" while the Amazon burned.

Lula did not address the criticism but said in a video posted Saturday on X that he had spoken with Amazonas Gov. Roberto Cidade and that the federal government was sending resources to support firefighting efforts.
Brazilian firefighters light the area of a wildfire in the Amazon rainforest in Iranduba, Brazil, on Sept. 30. (Michael Dantas/AFP/Getty)
"The people of Amazonas can count on the federal government. We are together in this fight to protect lives, preserve the forest and support those facing this emergency," the president said.

Susana Braz, a 35-year-old biologist in Manaus who studies how toxic ash from Amazon wildfires affects the region's rivers, said she could not sleep in her own bed because her smoke-filled bedroom felt like a barbecue grill.
- Climate change past the point of no return, UN says, as worst impacts are now unavoidable
- Lula and Bolsonaro head to run-off in Brazil's presidential election
"We come home, and the house is full of smoke," Braz said. "We go outside, and there's smoke everywhere."

People have tried to carry on as usual, but worsening smoke over the past week and a half has fuelled frustration. "Are we really going to accept this smoke as normal, as if everything is fine and we just have to live with it?" she added.
The Jornalista Phelippe Daou Bridge is shrouded in smoke from wildfires in Manaus, Brazil, on Oct. 9. (Edmar Barros/The Associated Press)

The Amazon stores vast amounts of carbon and releases moisture that regulates weather far beyond South America. But climate change and deforestation are making it hotter, drier and more flammable. El Niño, a recurring climate pattern, can also worsen heat and drought.

"Nearly all ignitions in the region are caused by human activity, mainly to renew pastures or clear land," said Ane Alencar, science director at Brazil's nonprofit Amazon Environmental Research Institute. "During very dry periods, those fires can escape."
Fire counts were expected to increase at this time of year with a developing El Niño, but the timing around elections is still notable, Alencar said Thursday.
"Over the past 10 days, we've seen fire hot spots nearly triple compared with the 10 days before the election, mainly around Manaus," she said. "Something happened that led people to burn more."
A group of women wear masks to protect themselves from smoke caused by wildfires in Manaus, Brazil, on Oct. 9. (Edmar Barros/The Associated Press)

João Morita, a co-ordinator at ICMBio, the federal agency that manages Brazil's protected areas, has been on the front lines fighting fires in conservation areas in the Amazon. He said several factors could explain last week's spike in the region, including residents of national forests burning crop plots, despite a ban.

"Fires start for all sorts of reasons. Some are retaliation for enforcement actions. Others are deliberately set with malicious intent. Any unauthorized burning is a crime, so there is a range of possibilities," Morita said.
Officials and researchers have warned that El Nino's effects on the Amazon could be worse in 2027 than this year.
A Brazilian firefighter rests in Iranduba, Brazil, on Sept. 30. (Michael Dantas/AFP/Getty)

articles.title: At least 16 people rescued off Mexico's Baja Coast, no sign of boat, says U.S. Coast Guard

paras.en: At least 16 people rescued off Mexico's Baja Coast, no sign of boat, says U.S. Coast Guard
One person who was rescued said as many as 27 people were on board

At least 16 people seen floating in the Pacific Ocean off Mexico's Baja California coast were rescued in the pre-dawn hours of Friday and authorities were searching for several others, a U.S. Coast Guard official said.
Petty Officer Chris Sappey said at about 1 a.m. PT, several people were spotted floating in the water about 225 kilometres west of Ensenada.

It was unclear why the people were in the water and no vessel has been found, Sappey said. He said one person who was rescued said as many as 27 people were on board a boat. He had no further details about what the people were doing.
"There was no sight of a vessel in the water, just straight people in the water," Sappey said.
Those being rescued were being taken to hospitals in San Diego, Sappey said.
The U.S. Coast Guard was assisting Mexican authorities in the search efforts with a helicopter, a fixed-airwing plane and a cutter, Sappey said.
- Mothers crossing the Mexico-U.S. border risk everything to reunite with their children
- Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts

Migrants are increasingly turning to the risky alternative offered by smugglers to travel by sea to avoid heavily guarded land borders, including off California's coast. Panga boats leave Mexico in the dead of night and sometimes chart hundreds of kilometers north.
There have been several incidents in recent years of migrant vessels capsizing en route to California.

In May 2025, at least three people died when a panga flipped off the coast, about 56 kilometres north of the U.S.-Mexico border. In 2023, eight people were killed when two migrant-smuggling boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog and one of them capsized in the surf. It was one of the deadliest maritime smuggling incidents in waters off the U.S. coast.

A federal judge sentenced a San Diego man to 18 years in prison in 2022 for piloting a small vessel overloaded with 32 migrants that smashed apart in powerful surf off the coast, killing three people and injuring more than two dozen.

articles.title: Houthi attacks on strategic Saudi assets threaten Riyadh's regional leadership and economic ambitions

paras.en: As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen continues to escalate, Saudi Arabia's most important national priorities are increasingly at risk. On Tuesday, the Houthis hit the headquarters of Aramco, the Saudi state-owned oil company in Dhahran. On Wednesday, the Houthis vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, and on Thursday a cruise missile was intercepted over the Medina region. While it remains unclear who launched it, the mere attempt raises questions about Saudi Arabia's role as guardian of Islam's holiest places, the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Following last weekend's Houthi attacks that killed more than a dozen people and injured more than 300 at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, tourists and potential investors are keenly aware of the growing uncertainty over travel and security in the kingdom.

Several airlines suspended flights to Riyadh and the airport was expected to remain closed through at least October 17, according to media reports published earlier this week. Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, an economic summit that usually draws foreign leaders and key players in business to the country, plans to offer remote participation instead of hosting attendees on site.

"The hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi government challenge Riyadh's image of stability and security amid the wider US-Iran war," said Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Washington-based think tank Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.

"The attacks on Saudi Arabia also threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify the economy," Kaldas told DW, noting that these ambitions depend on potential tourists viewing the kingdom as a safe destination.

Since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, Tehran, and later the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, have been targeting Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States. Saudi Arabia also supports the Yemeni government in its fight against the Houthis with airstrikes in Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
Houthi attacks are a blow to Saudi Arabia's ambitions
A decade ago, Saudi Arabia launched Vision 2030, a sweeping economic and social reform plan, to reduce the kingdom's reliance on oil and transform its economy and society.

"Saudi Arabia is pursuing a highly nationalist 'Saudi-First' policy, aimed at propelling the nation to the global forefront as an aviation power, a hub for artificial intelligence and a major tourism destination," Simon Wolfgang Fuchs, a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told DW.
Fuchs views the Houthi attacks as a significant blow to these ambitions and the financial resources available to pursue them.

Pauline Raabe, a senior analyst at the Berlin-based Middle East Minds think tank, points out that Saudi Arabia urgently needs to find a solution that shields its population from the conflict while limiting the economic damage and reputational costs.

"It is a race against time," she told DW, even though the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is no new occurence. Saudi Arabia supported the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022.
"The conflict has been flaring up again with renewed intensity due to the general situation in the Gulf and is as such actually a tightening of the status quo," Raabe said.
However, she views Saudi Arabia's loss of authority as a threat on the horizon. "In the short term, Saudi Arabia is a belligerent [player] in a region ravaged by conflict," she said.
Symbolic support from partners like Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt

"Riyadh remains a key player through its investments, its position as the world's largest oil exporter and its role as custodian of Islam's holy sites in Mecca and Medina," he said, adding that "by virtue of this role, Saudi Arabia can count on allies and call for the formation of alliances."

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. While the latter two have since offered intelligence and defense support for Saudi Arabia, they also made clear that they will not put boots on the ground in Yemen. France and the United Kingdom also offered limited defense support for Riyadh. Egypt, the most populous Arab country with a Sunni majority like Saudi Arabia, voiced verbal support.
"Riyadh is prioritizing the symbolic value of these countries, projecting an image of strong ties with regional powers," Kaldas said.

However, much attention has focused on Saudi Arabia's failure to secure defense support from the United States, he added. While Saudi Arabia's closest ally — the US signaled willingness to support Riyadh with intelligence sharing and targeting assistance against the Houthis — Washington has so far stopped short of committing US forces to direct strikes. For Saudi Arabia, the understanding is therefore that the US prioritzes avoiding opening another front in the regional conflict against Iran.

articles.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama

paras.en: The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution." The protests began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.
The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down. They say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. local time on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.
"These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the EU. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.
"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

articles.title: Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women

paras.en: The life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end in the early hours of October 5, when the 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.
Media reported that about 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.

What the young woman's relatives considered her guilty of has not been publicly reported. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.

In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter, or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.

What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or local social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.

For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.

Moghaddam stressed that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."

Iran's laws, based on the interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.

Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.

These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.

According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.

In Maryam Yarmohammadi's case, it was above all the extraordinary brutality of the crime that shocked the public. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."

At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, holding the victim responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."

Psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh argues that, for years, men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions. Male identity, she said, is simultaneously tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh explained.

"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power. Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."

Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz believes that women understand the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, have achieved significant progress over the past decades.

Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.

"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," said Rangriz. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet hardly anyone asks what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Division in Lebanon over Hezbollah’s confiscated explosives

paras.en: Beirut, Lebanon – On October 5, a minivan was stopped at a checkpoint in Dahr el-Baydar between the Bekaa Valley and Mount Lebanon region.
Lebanese security forces discovered the car was carrying hundreds of kilos of explosive materials, including TNT and C-4, according to Lebanese officials.

On Thursday, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah released a statement saying that the explosives belonged to Hezbollah which had demanded their return, along with the release of the two people detained in the vehicle.

“From the moment the vehicle was detained, the relevant bodies within [Hezbollah] immediately contacted the security and judicial agencies and informed them that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the resistance,” Fadlallah said in his statement. “They demanded the immediate release of those detained and the return of the vehicle and everything inside it, as these are capabilities used by the resistance to confront the Israeli occupation of our land in the south [of Lebanon].”

Fadlallah indicated that the explosives were for use against Israel, which continues to occupy large parts of southern Lebanon, and not internally against the Lebanese government or other factions, as some political figures and analysts had suggested.

“We therefore warn the [Lebanese] authorities of the consequences of continuing to escalate their measures,” he said. “[Hezbollah] will defend its people’s rights and the capabilities it uses to confront the Israeli enemy and it will not tolerate any targeting by any party implementing American demands against our resistance.”

But many of Hezbollah’s political opponents, who blame the Iranian-backed group for targeting political opponents in assassinations in the past, fear that smuggled explosives will be turned against Hezbollah’s detractors.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pointed out that C-4 explosives had been used in previous assassinations, although investigators have not established that the seized shipment was intended for such an attack.
Hezbollah has never admitted carrying out assassinations, despite repeated accusations against it, including the killing of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005.

On March 2, when Hezbollah responded to ongoing Israeli attacks for the first time in over a year in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Salam and his government banned the group’s military activities. Salam’s coalition government includes two Hezbollah ministers who opposed the decision and the group has repeatedly defied the government’s declaration by continuing to fight Israel.

Fighting has largely subsided since June, when Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-administered trilateral framework agreement. Under the deal, pilot zones would be established as part of a phased process in which Israel would eventually withdraw its troops and the Lebanese Army would enter to disarm Hezbollah. However, the programme has had complications from the start as Israel never had a presence in some of the areas included in the pilot zones, according to locals, and Israeli demolitions continue in the areas under its occupation.

paras.en: In recent weeks, Lebanese security forces have uncovered a number of operations aimed at smuggling explosives.
Lebanese officials have condemned the smuggling operations and Salam has vowed to investigate the incidents, particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident.

“We will not be lenient in following up and expanding the investigation in order to identify all those involved in this criminal operation and those behind them,” Salam wrote on social media. “We will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness.”
But the issue also points to growing disagreements between Lebanon’s government and Hezbollah’s leadership over the role of armed resistance.

Since the end of Lebanon’s civil war in 1990, Hezbollah has been the principal Lebanese force to keep its weapons. This was ostensibly part of a national security formula of “the army, the people and the resistance” aimed at opposing Israeli occupation – which continued until 2000 before resuming in 2024 – and aggression, while the country was also under Syrian hegemony.

That changed last year when President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Salam came to power. The Hezbollah allied al-Assad regime in Damascus had just fallen, cutting off a powerful land route of weapons and financing from Tehran. The regional power dynamic appeared to be shifting towards a decrease in Iranian power and more influence from the United States and Israel, leading Lebanon’s leaders to announce that all non-state weapons would come under control of the state.

Despite Hezbollah’s opposition to the new leaders’ decrees, the Lebanese Army went about disarming Hezbollah sites in southern Lebanon. Some Hezbollah opponents have declared the group weak and defeated, though analysts say the group still retains some fighting power and that Lebanon’s regional alliances could largely be determined by regional events.
Still, the group’s domestic influence has been challenged at times by the new Lebanese leadership, including in the Dahr el-Baydar incident.

Marcel Baloukji, a former brigadier general who oversaw the Lebanese Army’s border committee with Syria, told Al Jazeera that the recent busts, and particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident, were connected to the security situation in the wider region, particularly concerning the US-Israeli war on Iran and the recent intensification of violence between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

He suggested that Hezbollah could be looking to follow the lead of other pro-Iranian actors in the region and intensify attacks against adversaries. But he also added that Hezbollah may need explosives for drones to attack Israeli forces occupying southern Lebanon.
Despite the promises by Lebanese officials to investigate, analysts said concerns remain about how effective the investigations might be.

Issam Kayssi, a Beirut-based analyst at the Carnegie Middle East Center, raised questions over Salam’s relationship with the Lebanese security apparatus. Lebanon has multiple security agencies, some of which have competing loyalties to different political figures or parties.

“We are more than a year on from the Raouche incident,” he said, referring to a Hezbollah event held on Beirut’s seafront in 2025 to commemorate the assassination of the group’s late leaders Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine. Hezbollah projected the likeness of the two slain leaders on Pigeon Rock in Beirut’s Raouche seafront district, despite the projections being prohibited by authorities, prompting Salam to call for the arrest of those responsible. Security agents on site failed to act to prevent the projections and observers fear that elements of the security agencies may not be fully cooperative with Salam in the explosives investigations he ordered.
